summary: Describes steps an implementation can take between receiving user input and handing permitted code points to the IDNA2008 protocol, since IDNA2008 itself assumes input is already from a permitted set. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a typed domain name can be handed to the IDNA2008 protocol, something has to tidy it up: fold capitals, widen characters, and put accents back together. This memo describes a four-step baseline for that work, and then warns that no one mapping suits every user.

questions: how to normalize user input for idna
how to normalize domain names for idna
full width half width characters idna
subtitle: How to normalize the characters a user types before they reach the IDNA2008 protocol.

tldr.problem: IDNA2008 expects input that has already been reduced to a permitted set of characters, but it does not say how to turn what users actually type into that form.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives a baseline of four ordered steps: map uppercase characters to lowercase, expand fullwidth and halfwidth characters, normalize the result to Unicode Normalization Form C, and map the ideographic full stop to the ASCII full stop before labels are split.
tldr.outcome: The authors do not recommend adopting the baseline unchanged. A real mapping has to account for locale, input method and user expectations, and the document says so in unusually direct terms.

today: RFC 5895 is an Informational document from September 2010, published as an independent submission rather than through an IETF stream. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It describes a user interface operation rather than a protocol on the wire, so it is guidance for applications to adapt rather than a specification a router implements.

sections.title: What This Document Does and Does Not Cover
sections.content:
In the original version of the Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) protocol, any Unicode code points taken from user input were mapped into a set of Unicode code points that made sense, then encoded and passed to the Domain Name System (DNS). The IDNA2008 protocol, described in RFCs 5890, 5891, 5892 and 5893, presumes that the input already comes from a set of permitted code points, which it then encodes and passes to the DNS, but does not specify what to do with the result of user input. This document describes the actions an implementation can take between receiving user input and passing permitted code points to the new protocol.

This is not a protocol that appears on the wire. It describes an operation applied to user input to prepare that input for use in an on-the-network protocol. The document says this is unusual for an Internet protocol document, and explains that it is needed for implementors who may have designed around the original IDNA protocol, referred to here as IDNA2003, which folds this user-input operation into the protocol itself.

Many valid mappings of characters from user input are possible. The mapping described here is the basis for other mappings and is not likely to be useful without modification. A useful mapping has features designed to reduce the surprise for users, and is likely to differ depending on the locale of the user, the type of input being used, such as typing, copy-and-paste or voice, and the type of application used. Most common mappings will probably produce similar results for the same input, but there will be subtle differences between applications.
sections.plainLanguage: IDNA2008 only accepts characters from an approved list, and it leaves it to the application to get user input onto that list. This memo describes how to do that, and is clear that the description is a starting point rather than a finished answer, because people type in different ways and expect different results.

sections.title: The Line Between User Interface and Protocol
sections.content:
The user interface of an application is more complicated than most network implementers think. When a user enters an internationalized domain name, that covers the whole chain: the user forming the name and choosing symbols to express it, entering those symbols with a keyboard, stylus or voice recognition program, the computer interpreting the input as scan codes, a graphical representation or digitized sounds, and finally normalizing those symbols into a character repertoire in an encoding that IDNA processes and the DNS recognise.

A user interface for internationalized domain names has to take account of culture, context and locale. The document gives a well-known example: lowercasing the letter LATIN CAPITAL LETTER I (U+0049). In Turkish and other languages a capital I lowercases to LATIN SMALL LETTER DOTLESS I (U+0131), not to LATIN SMALL LETTER I (U+0069). That lowercasing depends on the locale of the system or of the user, so a single context-free mapping has the potential of doing exactly the wrong thing.

The original IDNA conflated user interface processing and protocol. It took whatever characters the user produced in whatever encoding the application used, assumed a conversion to Unicode code points, and then, without regard to context, locale or the user's intentions, mapped them into a particular set of other characters and re-encoded them in Punycode, so the whole operation sat inside the protocol. Ignoring context, locale and user preference made life simpler for the application developer, at the cost of violating the principle of least user surprise for consumers and producers of domain names.

In IDNA2008 the dividing line is clear. The specification defines the protocol part and explicitly does not deal with the user interface. A mapping such as the one here deals with the user interface and not the protocol. A mapping is only applied before a string of characters is treated as a domain name, in the user interface, and is never applied during domain name processing, in the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Typing a name is not one step. The person chooses the symbols, an input method turns them into characters, and the application then has to tidy the result. Where that tidying happens matters: doing it inside the protocol, as the original IDNA did, forces one rule on every language and every input method, and the wrong rule is as likely as the right one.

sections.title: The Four Ordered Mapping Steps
sections.content:
The general algorithm an application, or the input method provided by an operating system, ought to use has four steps, and they are applied in order.

First, uppercase characters are mapped to their lowercase equivalents using the algorithm for mapping case in Unicode characters. The step was chosen because the output behaves more like ASCII host names behave.

Second, fullwidth and halfwidth characters, those defined with Decomposition Types <wide> and <narrow>, are mapped to their decomposition mappings as shown in the Unicode character database. The step was chosen because many input mechanisms, particularly in Asia, do not allow the user to enter characters in the form IDNA2008 requires, and because even where they do, the user may not know which form they are entering.

Third, all characters are mapped using Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC). The step was chosen because it maps combinations of combining characters into canonical composed form. Users are not generally aware of the particular form of the characters they are entering, and IDNA2008 requires that only the canonical composed forms from NFC be used.

Fourth, IDNA2008 acts on the individual labels of the domain name. An implementation of this mapping that also performs the separation of the parts of a domain name into labels using the FULL STOP character (U+002E) can map the IDEOGRAPHIC FULL STOP character (U+3002) to the FULL STOP before label separation occurs. Other characters used as full stops could be considered for mapping as label separators, but their use as such has not been investigated thoroughly. Only U+3002 is added, because the authors have not fully investigated the applicability of other characters and the environments in which they should and should not be considered label separators. The step was chosen because some input mechanisms do not allow the user to enter proper label separators.

Definitions for the rules in the algorithm are found in the Unicode Standard, Version 5.2.0. Unicode Normalization Form C is in Annex 15 of the Unicode Standard Annex #15. To map uppercase characters to their lowercase equivalents, first map characters to the Lowercase_Mapping property if any, then map characters to the Simple_Lowercase_Mapping property if any. To map fullwidth and halfwidth characters to their decomposition mappings, map any character whose Decomposition_Type is either <wide> or <narrow> to the Decomposition_Mapping of that character. If the mappings in this document are applied to versions of Unicode later than 5.2, the later versions of the Unicode Standard should be consulted. These form a minimal set of mappings an application should strongly consider doing, and there are many others that might be done.
sections.plainLanguage: Four steps, in this order: fold capitals to lowercase, widen out fullwidth and halfwidth characters, put combining marks back into one composed character, and treat the ideographic full stop as an ordinary dot before the name is split into labels. Each step exists because a real input method produces a form the protocol would otherwise reject, and the user cannot tell which form they typed.

sections.title: Implementing the Mapping in an Application
sections.content:
If you are implementing a mapping for an application or operating system by using exactly the four steps above, the authors have a request: please do not. They mean it. The four steps do not describe a universal mapping algorithm, because there is no universally applicable mapping algorithm.

If you read the material in the algorithm without reading the introduction, the authors ask you to go back and read it carefully, because in many ways the introduction is more important. Further, you can probably think of user interface considerations that the document did not list. And if you read the introduction and decided that the algorithm is completely correct for the intended users of your application or operating system, the authors say you are probably not thinking hard enough about your intended users.

The mapping described here was designed to be sensible and friendly and mostly obvious to people throughout the world when using typical applications with domain names entered by hand, and to let applications be mostly backwards compatible with IDNA2003. By definition it cannot meet all of those design goals for all people, and it is known to fail on some of them for quite large populations of people.

A good mapping in the real world might use the same design goal but a different algorithm. Many algorithms will produce results close to what is described, but will differ in assumptions about how users think and type. A mapping might apply to a spoken user interface rather than a typed one. A mapping might be different for users typing than for users copying and pasting from other applications. And a user interface that accepts typed input transliterated from Latin characters could have very different mappings from one that applies to typing in other character sets, which would be typical of a Pinyin input method for Chinese characters.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors are unusually blunt: do not implement these four steps as they stand. The steps are a floor, not a ceiling. An application has to know who its users are, because the same typed characters mean different things in different languages, and a copy-and-paste action delivers a different string than typing does.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document suggests creating mappings that might cause confusion for some users while alleviating confusion in other users. Such confusion is not covered in any depth in this document, nor in the other IDNA-related documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Any mapping trades one kind of confusion for another. Two users who mean the same name can end up with different strings, and two different names can end up looking the same. The document says it does not cover this in depth.

viz.caption: THE FOUR MAPPING STEPS, IN THE ORDER THEY MUST BE APPLIED

items.label: Uppercase to lowercase
items.desc: So the output behaves more like ASCII host names behave.

items.label: Fullwidth and halfwidth to decomposition
items.desc: Many input mechanisms do not let the user enter the form IDNA2008 requires.

items.label: Normalization Form C
items.desc: Combines combining characters into canonical composed form, which IDNA2008 requires.

items.label: Ideographic full stop to full stop
items.desc: Some input mechanisms do not let the user enter a proper label separator. Applied before label separation.

viz.caption: WHERE THE MAPPING BELONGS IN IDNA2008

left.title: User interface
left.desc: The mapping is applied here, before a string of characters is treated as a domain name.

right.title: Protocol
right.desc: Domain name processing happens here, and a mapping is never applied at this stage.
